compliance.notes: Re-scored on BCP's complete 2026/27 pack after the capital and budget documents were supplied by hand; the earlier assessment_caveat is CLEARED (explicit "") because the capital-strategy content is now in evidence and the residual gaps are BCP's, not ours. BCP publishes no standalone capital strategy: its capital strategy is a section of the Cabinet budget report of 11 February 2026 (paras 66-82, 'The capital strategy is based on the following core principles'), with the Capital Investment Programme (Appendices 7 and 7a) and the 2026-2031 Strategic Asset Management Plan (Appendix 8) as its substance, all recommended to full Council (recommendations viii-x, unchanged by the 10 February addendum). STRONGEST: the liability benchmark (separate General Fund and HRA charts plotting all four balances to 2095); the capital expenditure / financing / CFR chain (five-year GF and HRA tables in the TMS, reconciled to a four-year programme by directorate and by scheme); the borrowing strategy and its candid handling of the projected over-borrowed position driven by cash-flowing the DSG/SEND deficit; the MRP policy (annuity asset-life, £12.8m of VRP overpayments disclosed); the creditworthiness policy (ratings plus a CDS overlay); and the S151 officer's s25 affordability and reserves advice. WEAKEST, and now confirmed as real gaps rather than missing documents: no financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio for either fund (PI-07), no upper/lower limits on the maturity structure of borrowing (PI-09) and no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02) — three core indicators absent from a 'Treasury Indicators' section that sets only the operational boundary and the authorised limit (and those as a single combined line, in a table headed £'000 whose figures are £m). On the commercial side the supplied capital documents confirm that BCP holds non-treasury investments (investment properties within a £2.16bn estate, council-owned companies and joint ventures, a £15.3m development exposure at Carters Quay) but nowhere quantifies them: no proportionality test against reserves (COM-03, core), no schedule of non-treasury investments by purpose (COM-04), no net commercial/service income ratio (PI-08) and no income-dependence or contingency disclosure (COM-07). Also absent: the promised specified/non-specified investment sections (INV-05), a portfolio risk-exposure indicator (INV-06), any derivatives policy (RISK-06) and any flag on audit qualification of the source data (RPT-05). The Treasury Management Policy, Practices and Schedules document (TMS para 82, 'will be presented alongside') is not in the pack, which limits TMP-01 and GOV-02 but nothing core.

gaps.evidence: TMS p.16 para 80 'The maximum period for investments will be 5 years'; p.15 para 75 sets time limits by counterparty type (local authorities 5 years, Banks 1 higher quality 2 years, Banks 1 medium quality 1 year, DMADF 6 months).
TMS p.10 para 59 reproduces the substance of Prudential Code para 51 and Budget report p.20 para 67 commits every borrowing-funded business case to the PWLB borrowing restrictions.

TMS p.24 Appendix 3: the S151 officer is responsible for 'ensuring the proportionality of all investments so that the Authority does not undertake a level of investing which exposes the Authority to an excessive level of risk compared to its financial resources'; TMS p.6 para 32 asks members, by approving the CFR figures, to 'consider the scale proportionate to the Council's remaining activity'; Budget report p.37 acknowledges exposure to council-owned companies and joint ventures.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council forecasts schools deficit of £275.5m by March 2027, with SEND reform plan awaiting approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects its dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m, according to its first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) to the Council meeting on 13 October. The in-year shortfall is projected at £95.7m. The DSG is the government grant that funds schools, and the deficit sits in its high needs part, which pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The report says the high-needs budget is £68.4m and spending is more than double that. The council calls the deficit "the Council's biggest financial risk" and the "most significant threat to the Council's long-term financial sustainability".

The council's main mitigation is a local SEND reform plan, submitted to government in June, with the outcome still awaited when the report was written. If it is approved, a High Needs Stability Grant would cover 90% of the deficit as it stood at 31 March 2026, with payment expected in autumn 2026. That is roughly £162m of about £180m. The report expects further support for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits. Alongside this, the capital programme (planned spending on things that last) includes £4.59m, not yet committed, for special and alternative provision, plus SEND resource schemes at St Clements/St John's (£815k), Pokesdown Primary (£450k) and Muscliffe Primary (£250k).

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council forecasts £275.5m schools deficit by March 2027; government grant covering 90% awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects the accumulated deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m at the start of the year. The first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) puts the deficit for 2026/27 alone at £95.7m. It is driven by the cost of placements for children with special educational needs and disabilities, which the council identifies as its most significant financial risk.

A new high needs stability grant, announced in the 2026/27 local government settlement, is intended to cover 90% of the deficit as it stood on 31 March 2026. It depends on government approving the council's local SEND reform plan, which was submitted in June; the outcome is awaited. If approved, the grant would be paid in autumn 2026. Government has also said it expects to offer similar support for further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, though not without limit, and that from 2028/29 SEND funding is expected to rise to fully fund expected spending.

The reform plan also carries capital spending (money spent on things that last) of £13.5m for 2026/27, made up of £8.9m of high needs grant and £4.6m of Special and Alternative Provision grant. The capital investment report says £4.1m of the high needs grant is "yet to be allocated to specific projects", and the Special and Alternative Provision money is not yet committed to approved schemes. Spending in the first quarter was £163,940. The council expects works to proceed through the summer and autumn holidays.

news_drafts.headline: BCP schools deficit forecast at £275.5m by March 2027; grant for 90% of existing gap awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP) Council expects its deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, to reach £275.5m by 31 March 2027, up from £179.8m a year earlier. A deficit on the grant is an overspend, usually on support for children with special needs. The Schools Forum was told the gap on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), is £95.7m for 2026-27, in line with the original budget. Other parts of the grant are forecast to balance.

The government has offered a stability grant covering 90% of the deficit at 31 March 2026, about £161.8m, to be paid in autumn 2026 if approved. It depends on government approval of BCP's local SEND reform plan, submitted in June; the outcome is awaited. The government has said there should be no further deficits beyond March 2028, as funding from 2028-29 rises to cover expected spending, with details due in the 2027 Spending Review. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such a deficit off the council's main balance sheet, also runs until 31 March 2028.

The yearly gap has grown from £49.7m in 2024-25 to £71.6m in 2025-26. Spending on independent and non-maintained special schools has risen from £30.2m to £49.3m over the period. The reform plan aims to shift investment towards early intervention, and a newly established High Needs Block Board oversees the deficit recovery plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Cyber security risk framed as a primary driver of investment urgency alongside standard asset lifecycle replacement
findings.detail: Council emphasises that aging and unsupported infrastructure materially increases exposure to cyber attacks, a growing threat to public sector. End-user laptops identified as critical frontline of cyber resilience; outdated devices reduce effectiveness of security controls and increase vulnerability exposure.
findings.matters: This frames the investment as compliance and operational risk mitigation, not optional modernisation; underpins rejection of 'do nothing' option; relevant to lenders assessing council's risk management posture
findings.figures: ~4,000 laptop devices; 6,500 users; UK experiencing 'regular, significant cyber incidents' at national level targeting public sector organisations
findings.quote: At the same time, the Council is operating in an environment of significantly heightened cyber risk. Public sector organisations continue to be a primary target for cyber-attacks and maintaining legacy or unsupported systems materially increases the Council's exposure to security vulnerabilities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Council acknowledges significant cost estimate uncertainty in final three years of programme (2030–2032) due to technology change and evolving cyber threats
findings.detail: Cost forecasts carry highest confidence in 2027/28 and 2028/29, based on known asset lifecycles and committed delivery plans. Later years subject to material uncertainty from rapid AI adoption increasing compute and storage demand, escalating cyber security requirements driving reactive investment, and broader technology sector volatility.
findings.matters: Six-year budget envelope may require upward revision in future years; peers and lenders need visibility of this acknowledged uncertainty rather than treating the plan as a fixed commitment
findings.quote: Confidence in cost estimates is strongest in the initial years of the programme (particularly 2027/28 and 2028/29), where requirements are clearly defined and based on known asset lifecycles, supplier pricing and committed project delivery plans. As the programme progresses into later years, there is a greater degree of uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Most core IT infrastructure and ~4,000-device laptop estate approaching end of life and requiring replacement within the 6-year programme
findings.detail: Normal laptop refresh cycle is 4 years, aligned to supplier warranty periods; BCP sometimes extends to 5 years. After 4 years, devices out of warranty, failure rates increase substantially, and vendor support reduces. Core IT platforms (hosting, networking, telephony) also reaching end-of-life and requiring modernisation.
findings.matters: This is compulsory infrastructure maintenance spending to sustain operational capability and service delivery, not discretionary capital; failure to invest would increase reactive costs and service disruption
findings.figures: ~4,000 laptop devices in daily use; 6,500 users across all council sites and partner locations; normal 4-year refresh cycle (sometimes flexed to 5 years)
findings.quote: Over the next 6 years, most of the current IT infrastructure and laptop estate will, or already has, reached a point in its lifecycle where it needs to be refreshed or replaced, in line with normal asset management practices.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Council proposing £11.2m prudential borrowing for IT infrastructure capital programme 2026–2032, with total borrowing cost of £2.8m
findings.detail: Investment funded through prudential borrowing over a 5-year repayment period. Total borrowing cost £2.8m; net impact on Medium-Term Financial Plan is £1.7m (£1.1m already included in MTFP). Interest rates assumed at 5.34% for 2026/27, then forecast 4.8%, 4.2%, and 4.1% for later years.
findings.matters: Major new borrowing commitment with significant debt servicing implications affecting the council's financial sustainability and medium-term financial flexibility
findings.figures: £11.2 million total investment; £2.8 million borrowing cost; £1.7 million net MTFP growth
findings.quote: It is proposed that the IT infrastructure investment plan is funded from prudential borrowing. The total cost of prudential borrowing for the £11.2 million investment over 6 years is £2.8 million. As £1.1 million is already reflected in the MTFP, the growth from MTFP perspective is £1.7 million.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Council's IT infrastructure and laptop estate at or beyond end of supported lifecycle, creating cyber security exposure and service disruption risks
findings.detail: The council's current IT infrastructure and laptop estate has reached or exceeded its effective lifecycle. Without investment, the council faces increasing cyber security risk, rising maintenance costs, system performance degradation, and potential service disruption affecting delivery of critical services to residents. This is the stated driver for the £11.2m capital investment programme.
findings.matters: Aging infrastructure represents material financial and operational risk; demonstrates the necessity and urgency of the capital investment; relevant to lenders assessing whether the council is addressing legitimate infrastructure threats.
findings.figures: IT infrastructure supports approximately 6,500 users across multiple council sites
findings.quote: Without planned investment, the Council faces increasing cyber security risk, rising maintenance costs, reduced system performance and a higher likelihood of service disruption, impacting the delivery of critical services to residents.
